passage: In the sandpit of a São Paulo park, Priscila, five, had the red dump truck. Yesterday Sami had let her use his bucket all afternoon. Now Sami toddled over. Priscila pushed the truck straight to him. "Your turn!" Then Lucas came, the boy who never let anyone touch his digger. He reached for the truck. Priscila pulled it back. "No. You don't share." Lucas stamped. Priscila crossed her arms. "When you share, I share." She went back to building a sand road with Sami.

qa.q: Who had let Priscila use his bucket yesterday?
qa.a: Sami had let her use his bucket all afternoon.

qa.q: What was Priscila feeling when she pulled the truck back from Lucas?
qa.a: Priscila felt it was unfair and a little cross, remembering that Lucas never let anyone touch his digger.

qa.q: What could a parent say to help all three children?
qa.a: A parent could praise Priscila for sharing with Sami and suggest Lucas try sharing his digger, so everyone sees how sharing works both ways.

qa.q: How might Lucas feel when Priscila said no?
qa.a: Lucas felt frustrated and left out, stamping his foot, maybe not yet understanding why.

grounding: A young child shares with the friend who shared last time and refuses the one who never shares, showing early "you did for me, I do for you" fairness.

passage: At Sunflower playschool, Uma, five, had the big box of crayons. Himani, who'd given Uma her pink crayon on Monday, sat down beside her. Uma slid the box over. "You can use all of them." Then Tinku came, the boy who always hid the glue stick in his pocket. He grabbed for the blue. Uma covered the box with both hands. "You never give me glue!" The teacher knelt down. "Tinku, what could you do?" Tinku slowly took the glue stick from his pocket and held it out. Uma thought, then pushed the blue crayon toward him.

qa.q: What did Tinku always hide in his pocket?
qa.a: He always hid the glue stick in his pocket.

qa.q: Why did Uma cover the box with both hands?
qa.a: Uma felt cross and wronged because Tinku never shared the glue, so she didn't want to share with him.

qa.q: How did the teacher help, and why did it work?
qa.a: The teacher asked Tinku what he could do, so he offered the glue and Uma was happy to share back.

qa.q: How might Himani feel when Uma slid the box over?
qa.a: Himani probably felt happy and included, since her kindness on Monday came back to her.

grounding: A young child shares crayons with the friend who shared before and refuses the one who never does, until he offers something back.

passage:
Sunday
Today Mami cut the big mango for Ayesha and me. She gave me three slices and Ayesha only two. Ayesha didn't even notice. But I said, "That's not fair! Ayesha should get the same!" Mami laughed and said I was being funny. I wasn't. I kept thinking about it.
I also counted: Ayesha helped me with my kite on Friday, and I helped her with her maths on Saturday. So we're even. Last week Rahim from next door borrowed my bat twice and never lent me his cricket ball once. I have written that down.
Mami says I'm like a shopkeeper. But I think things should be equal. Otherwise it feels wrong in my tummy.
- Samir

qa.q: How many mango slices did Samir get?
qa.a: Samir got three slices.

qa.q: Why did Samir object to getting more mango?
qa.a: Samir felt it was unfair and uncomfortable, a wrong feeling in the tummy, because things should be equal even when Samir gets the extra.

qa.q: What could Mami say to help Samir think about fairness?
qa.a: Mami could praise Samir for caring about fairness, and gently explain that not every kindness needs to be counted exactly.

qa.q: How might Ayesha see Samir's objection?
qa.a: Ayesha didn't even notice the unequal split, so she might be surprised Samir cared so much.

grounding: A child keeps score of favours and objects to an unequal split even when getting the extra, showing an emerging, rigid sense of fairness.

passage: At the temple fair in their village, Jyoti's uncle bought kulfi for the children and gave Keerthana, nine, two sticks and Jyoti only one. "Keerthana helped carry the water pots," he said. Keerthana frowned. "But Jyoti carried the flowers. That's the same work." She held out one kulfi to Jyoti. Jyoti shook her head. "Keep it, you like pista." Keerthana stamped her foot. "No! It has to be equal." Jyoti's uncle laughed. "Such a strict judge!" But Keerthana kept holding it out until Jyoti took it. Then she counted who had carried what at the fair all morning, on her fingers, just to be sure.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel about Keerthana's strict fairness?
qa.a: Jyoti seemed amused and generous, happy to let Keerthana keep it, maybe a bit surprised by how much it mattered to her friend.

grounding: A child objects loudly to an unequal kulfi split even when she gets the extra, and keeps score of who did what, showing a rigid sense of fairness.

passage: In their Mexico City classroom, Camila, eleven, and her group got their project back: an A. The teacher said the group could split ten bonus stickers however they liked. Olga said, "Camila did the most. She should get four." Camila shook her head hard. "No, it should be even. Two each, and I have a list." She pulled out a notebook: who drew the map, who wrote the report, who brought glue. "Olga did the map. Ben did the cover." The others groaned. "You don't have to be so exact," Ben said. Camila's cheeks went pink. "But it's not fair if it's not fair." The teacher smiled. "Camila, you care a lot about fairness. That's good. Maybe fairness can have a little space for thank-yous too."

qa.q: How many bonus stickers could the group split?
qa.a: They could split ten bonus stickers.

qa.q: How did Camila feel when Ben said she didn't have to be so exact?
qa.a: Camila felt embarrassed and stubborn, cheeks going pink, sure that fairness mattered.

qa.q: What does the teacher's comment help Camila see?
qa.a: That caring about fairness is good, but fairness can also leave room for generosity and thank-yous.

qa.q: How might Olga have felt when Camila refused the extra stickers?
qa.a: Olga may have felt surprised and a little frustrated, since she was trying to thank Camila.

grounding: A child keeps a list of who helped and insists on equal shares even when offered the extra, showing a sometimes rigid sense of fairness.

passage: Varun, you asked why I always return favours so fast? Let me tell you. I'm Ira nani. When I was fifteen, in Allahabad, my friend Kamala lent me her history notes for the whole year, because I was sick for two months. I passed because of those notes. Then, before the finals, Kamala asked me to help her with maths. I was busy preparing my own exams and said, "Later." Later never came. She failed maths. I kept telling myself it wasn't my fault. But every time I saw her, I felt guilty, as if I owed her a debt I hadn't paid. She stopped sitting with me. Years later I found her address and wrote to say sorry. She wrote back: "I never kept a list." I had. That was the sad part.

qa.q: How long was Ira sick?
qa.a: Ira was sick for two months.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling every time she saw Kamala?
qa.a: Ira felt guilty, as if carrying an unpaid debt.

qa.q: Why was writing to Kamala years later a turning point in the story?
qa.a: It let Ira finally admit the unpaid favour and apologise, easing the guilt and showing the ledger was mostly in Ira's head.

qa.q: How might Kamala have felt when Ira said "Later"?
qa.a: Kamala may have felt hurt and let down, having helped Ira all year.

grounding: An elder recalls feeling the pull to repay a friend's help and years of guilt when she didn't, showing how reciprocity binds and can become a ledger.

passage: The power had gone out across the colony the night before the physics exam, and Sachin, fifteen, was studying by a flickering candle. All term, Nitin had given him his neat notes whenever Sachin missed class for cricket. Now his phone buzzed: Nitin. "Can you explain optics? I'm totally lost." Sachin's battery was at ten percent, and he hadn't finished optics himself. He typed, "Sorry, I'm stuck too," then deleted it. He felt a hot knot of guilt; Nitin had never once said no to him. But helping would take an hour he didn't have. He stared at the candle. Then he called, and they worked through three diagrams over the phone until the battery died. Sachin went to bed with less revision but lighter in his chest.

qa.q: What had Nitin given Sachin all term?
qa.a: Nitin had given him his neat notes.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling when he deleted his message?
qa.a: Sachin felt a hot knot of guilt, aware that Nitin had never said no to him.

qa.q: Why did Sachin's choice to call feel right to him?
qa.a: It let him repay Nitin's help, easing the guilt and keeping the friendship balanced, even at a cost to his own revision.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel after the call?
qa.a: Nitin probably felt relieved and grateful that Sachin returned the help when he needed it.

grounding: A teenager who received notes all term feels a pull to return the favour and guilt if he doesn't, in a power cut the night before an exam.

passage: Tanuja, sixteen, had helped Chaitanya with maths every evening after school for a whole term, sitting at the colony's library table in Hyderabad. He'd scored ninety in the half-yearly. Now she needed help with her chemistry project, and he was the only one who knew how to use the lab software. "Can you help me Saturday?" she asked. "I'm busy. Maybe next week," he said, not looking up from his phone. Next week, he said the same. Tanuja started noticing every time he asked her for a maths answer. Each question felt like another coin in a box he never paid back. She felt resentful and a little stupid. At dinner she told her mother, "I think I've been keeping a list of everything I've done for him." Her mother said, "Then maybe it's time to tell him, not just count."

qa.q: What did Chaitanya score in the half-yearly?
qa.a: He'd scored ninety in the half-yearly.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when Chaitanya kept saying "next week"?
qa.a: Tanuja felt resentful and a little foolish, as if her help was never going to be returned.

qa.q: What does Tanuja's mother suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She suggests telling Chaitanya directly instead of silently counting, which could clear the resentment and give him a chance to reciprocate.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya see the situation?
qa.a: Chaitanya may not even realise how much Tanuja has done or how unfair his "next week" feels to her.

grounding: A teenager who helped a friend all term feels resentment when he doesn't return the favour, noticing that reciprocity has become a ledger.

passage:

Something's shifted in our flat and I just noticed it. There are four of us. Madhuri always uses everyone's shampoo, eats from our shelf, borrows chargers. She never buys the shared milk or cleans the stove. At first we all just laughed. This week, though, I noticed Priyanka moved her shampoo into her room. Ruchi stopped offering Madhuri a ride. Tonight, when Madhuri asked me for my notes, I said, "I'm using them," though I wasn't. Nobody has said anything to her face. But we've all quietly stopped. In the kitchen, Priyanka said, "She'll get the hint." I felt uneasy. Part of me thinks she deserves it. Part of me thinks we should just talk to her.

passage: At the polytechnic hostel in Hubli, Jahnavi, twenty, watched the scooter problem grow. Nitin borrowed someone's scooter almost every evening. passage:
Thursday
Covered Elizabeth's shift again today. That's the fourth time this month. She always has a reason: her cousin's wedding, a headache, a friend's party. And she never covers for anyone. When I asked her to swap Saturday, she said she "couldn't possibly."
I don't mind helping. I covered Ravi when his baby was born and I'd do it again. I helped the new girl with the billing system for a week and never expected anything. But Elizabeth takes and takes.
So today I told her, calmly, in the break room: "I've been happy to help. But I can't cover your shifts anymore unless you're able to cover mine sometimes." She looked shocked. I felt my heart pounding, but I didn't take it back. It felt fair.
- Ayesha

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel while telling Elizabeth the limit?
qa.a: Ayesha felt nervous, heart pounding, but steady and sure it was fair.

qa.q: What does Ayesha's approach show about healthy reciprocity?
qa.a: Ayesha stays generous with people who need help but calmly sets a limit with someone who habitually takes.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth have felt hearing Ayesha's limit?
qa.a: Elizabeth looked shocked, perhaps surprised that someone finally named the pattern.

grounding: A young adult helps colleagues generously without counting, but calmly stops giving to one who habitually takes and never returns the favour.

passage: In their village near Nashik, Arohi, twenty-five, kept a small shed of farm tools her late father had left. She lent them to anyone who asked: the widow next door, the schoolteacher, the boys fixing the temple roof. She never kept count. But Gautam, from the upper fields, was different. He borrowed the plough every season, returned it caked in mud, once with a cracked handle, and never lent her his tractor when she asked. This year he came again. Arohi's heart beat faster, but she kept her voice calm. "Gautam-bhai, I've lent you the plough six seasons. When I needed the tractor, you said no. I can't lend it again unless things go both ways." He looked annoyed. "It's just a plough." "Then you won't miss it," she said, and closed the shed door gently.

qa.q: How does Arohi show that generosity and limits can go together?
qa.a: She keeps lending freely to neighbours in need but refuses a habitual taker, explaining why calmly.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel being refused?
qa.a: Gautam seemed annoyed and perhaps embarrassed, used to getting the plough without giving back.

grounding: A young adult who lends her tools freely to neighbours calmly stops lending to one who habitually takes and never returns the favour.

Amma saw the girls under the slide and pulled Rekha onto her lap. "That hurt your heart, didn't it?" Rekha nodded. Amma held her until she stopped shaking, then took her to the swings.

passage: When I was eleven, my three best friends, including Naveen, suddenly stopped talking to me. No fight, no reason. One Monday I said "hi" and they looked through me like I was a window. But I stopped feeling like a ghost. I'm Jasleen, and I still remember that week.

passage: Gopika, you asked why I get upset when you talk about "not letting" a girl sit with your group. Let me tell you. I'm your Kunal mama. When I was eleven, there was a new boy, Manoj, who was good at everything, cricket, maths, jokes. My friends started liking him more than me. So I made a rule: nobody talks to Manoj. And they obeyed. Walking around with everyone doing what I said, I felt like a king. I told myself Manoj was a show-off who deserved it. But really, I was scared. If he took my place, where would I go? One day I saw him crying behind the bicycle shed. I felt sick. That evening I told my father, and he made me go to Manoj's house and apologise that same night. I've never forgotten either the power or the fear.

qa.q: What did Kunal tell his friends about Manoj?
qa.a: He made a rule: nobody talks to Manoj.

qa.q: What was Kunal really feeling behind the freeze-out?
qa.a: Kunal felt powerful, but underneath was scared of losing his place to Manoj.

qa.q: Why was going to Manoj's house to apologise a turning point in the story?
qa.a: It made Kunal face what he had done and take responsibility the same day, instead of hiding behind the story that Manoj deserved it.

qa.q: How might Manoj have experienced the freeze-out?
qa.a: Manoj likely felt hurt and lonely, which is why Kunal found him crying behind the bicycle shed.

grounding: An elder recalls leading a freeze-out of a classmate as a boy, feeling powerful while secretly fearing losing his own place.

passage: It was pouring on the school trip, and forty children were packed into one hall at the science museum, waiting for the rain to stop. Vasudha, ten, had spent the whole bus ride whispering to her group: "Don't sit with the new girl, Rhea. She thinks she's so smart." Now, in the hall, Rhea tried to join them on the mat. Vasudha shook her head, and the others turned their backs. Vasudha felt a little rush: they'd listened to her. Rhea sat alone near the door. Anand, from their class, looked at Vasudha. "Why are you doing this?" "She's a show-off," Vasudha said quickly. But the truth was, since Rhea came, Vasudha's best friend had started sitting with Rhea at lunch. Vasudha was afraid of being the one left out. The class teacher noticed Rhea alone and walked over.

qa.q: How many children were packed into the hall?
qa.a: Forty children were packed into one hall.

qa.q: What was Vasudha really afraid of?
qa.a: Vasudha was afraid of losing her best friend to Rhea and being the one left out herself.

qa.q: What could Vasudha do instead of freezing Rhea out?
qa.a: Vasudha could talk to her best friend about feeling left out, and include Rhea rather than turning others against her.

qa.q: What is it like for Rhea sitting alone near the door?
qa.a: Rhea likely feels hurt and lonely, shut out on a trip where everyone else has a group.

grounding: A child organises a group to shun a new classmate, feeling powerful while secretly afraid of losing her own place, during a rain-bound school trip.

passage: At the Lucknow colony's evening cricket, Preeti, eleven, stood by the stumps and announced, "Pankaj isn't playing. Nobody pass to him." The other kids nodded. Pankaj stood on the edge of the field, bat in hand. Preeti felt powerful. Everyone was listening to her. When her little cousin asked why, Preeti said, "He cheats." But she knew he didn't. The real reason was that yesterday, the older kids had picked Pankaj first instead of her, and she had felt, for a horrible moment, like she didn't belong. If he was out, she was safe. Pankaj walked home early, dragging his bat. Preeti watched him go and felt a strange twist in her stomach. Her grandmother, watching from the balcony, called her up and asked quietly, "What did that boy do?" Preeti had no answer.

qa.q: Why did Preeti say Pankaj couldn't play?
qa.a: Preeti said, "He cheats."

qa.q: What was Preeti really feeling behind the freeze-out?
qa.a: Preeti felt powerful on the surface but was afraid of not belonging after the older kids picked Pankaj first.

qa.q: What could Preeti's grandmother help her understand?
qa.a: Her grandmother could help Preeti see that excluding Pankaj came from fear, and encourage her to apologise and let him play.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have felt walking home early?
qa.a: Pankaj likely felt hurt and rejected, excluded without knowing the real reason.

grounding: A child who leads a group in shutting out a boy feels powerful but acts from fear of losing her own place, telling herself he deserves it.

passage:
Dear Naveen bhaiya,
You asked if school was better this term. Mostly. But I want to tell you something I noticed.
There's a boy in my class, Raju, who eats alone every day behind the water cooler. Last week I saw he'd been removed from the class group chat; someone made a new one without him. Nobody talked about it. He just stopped coming to the canteen.
I didn't want to make a big thing of it, like standing up in class. So on Monday I sat next to him at lunch and asked about his cricket bat. He looked surprised, then talked for ten minutes. On Wednesday I asked him to be in my project group. Two other guys joined us.
It's small. But he laughed today. I told our class teacher about the group chat too, so she's looking into it.
Vaibhav

qa.q: Where does Raju eat every day?
qa.a: He eats alone every day behind the water cooler.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when he noticed Raju had been left out?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt concerned and a little uneasy, wanting to help without drawing attention to Raju.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav's small acts work well?
qa.a: Sitting with Raju and including him in a project broke his isolation quietly, and telling the teacher about the chat brought an adult in.

qa.q: How might Raju feel after Vaibhav sat with him?
qa.a: Raju likely felt surprised and relieved, less lonely, which is why he laughed by the end of the week.

grounding: A student notices a classmate eating alone and dropped from the group chat, and small, quiet acts of inclusion begin to break the cycle.

passage: So, for the school podcast, I'm supposed to talk about kindness. I'm Ira, class ten. There's a girl in our class, Binita, who moved here from Guwahati. For a whole month she ate lunch alone on the steps near the library. I noticed she'd been dropped from our class chat when someone made a new one. Nobody said anything. I felt awful, but I also didn't want to make a scene. So one day I just sat down next to her on the steps with my tiffin. I didn't say "Are you okay?" or anything. I asked what she was reading. It was a mystery novel I liked. Now we eat together most days. Two other girls started joining us. It's not some big rescue. It's just lunch. But she told me last week it was the first time she felt like she belonged here.

qa.q: Where did Binita eat lunch alone?
qa.a: She ate lunch alone on the steps near the library.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when noticing Binita alone?
qa.a: Ira felt awful and concerned, but didn't want to make a scene.

qa.q: What makes Ira's approach effective?
qa.a: Ira simply sat down and asked about the book, a small, low-key act that included Binita without drawing attention.

qa.q: How did Binita experience Ira's small act?
qa.a: Binita felt she belonged for the first time, as she said last week.

grounding: A student notices a classmate eating alone and dropped from the group chat, and a small act of sitting with her breaks the cycle quietly.

passage: I'm Himani, and I sit two rows behind Elizabeth in class eleven. She joined from Shillong in July. By September, I noticed she ate lunch alone at the end of the bench. When the teacher asked us to form project groups, she was always the last one standing. I also noticed she wasn't in the new class chat someone had made. I can't say for sure how she felt. She mostly kept her head down, sometimes reading. But once I saw her check her phone, then put it away quickly, like she'd been hoping for a message. The next time groups were made, I just said, "Elizabeth, join us?" She looked up, surprised, and came over. I added her to the chat that evening. She didn't say much. But she stayed with our group at lunch the next day.

qa.q: Where did Elizabeth eat lunch alone?
qa.a: She ate lunch alone at the end of the bench.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling on seeing Elizabeth check her phone and put it away?
qa.a: Himani felt a pang of sympathy, sensing Elizabeth might be lonely and hoping for a message.

qa.q: Why was a simple "join us?" a good way to help?
qa.a: It included Elizabeth naturally in a task without singling her out, which made it easy for her to accept.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Elizabeth to be asked to join?
qa.a: Elizabeth was surprised and probably relieved, glad not to be the last one standing.

grounding: An observing classmate notices a new student eating alone and left out of chats, and a small invitation to a group breaks the cycle without drawing attention.

passage: In second year, Dilnaz's group stopped inviting me. There was no fight. Just one weekend they all went to Lonavala, and I saw the photos. Then another. By Diwali, I was out of their group chat. It hurt more than I'd admit. For a while I lay in my hostel bed thinking something must be wrong with me: too loud, too boring, too something. Then my roommate said, "Hafsa, you've been sad for weeks. Come to badminton." I went. I also started eating with the girls from my lab. I told my old school friend, on the phone, how much it had hurt, and just saying it helped. When Dilnaz later messaged about notes, I was tempted to ignore her the way they'd ignored me. I didn't. I sent the notes. I just didn't try to get back in. I'm Hafsa, and I'm okay now.

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz's group go one weekend?
qa.a: They all went to Lonavala.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel after being dropped from the group chat?
qa.a: Hafsa felt hurt and began to doubt, wondering whether something was wrong with Hafsa.

qa.q: Which of Hafsa's choices helped recovery, and why?
qa.a: Admitting the hurt, reaching out to new people like the lab group and badminton, and not retaliating let Hafsa rebuild without deciding something was wrong inside.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz have felt when Hafsa sent the notes?
qa.a: Dilnaz might have felt relieved and perhaps a little guilty, receiving kindness after shutting Hafsa out.

grounding: A young adult excluded from a friend circle admits the hurt, reaches out to others and avoids retaliating, recovering without deciding the fault lies within.

passage:
Hostel counsellor's note, Thursday.
Shankar (second-year) came in today. His old friend circle from first year has started excluding him: plans made without him, a trip he learned about from photos. He said he felt "like a door slammed." He also said, "Maybe I'm just annoying." We talked about how exclusion hurts like real pain, and that it doesn't prove anything is wrong with him. He's already started going to the photography club and has two new friends there. He admitted he'd thought about posting a photo from a party they weren't invited to, "to show them." He decided not to. He wants to stay polite with the old group without chasing them. I suggested he keep in touch with his school friends too. We'll meet in two weeks.
- Shalini, counsellor

qa.q: How did Shankar learn about the trip?
qa.a: He learned about it from photos.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling when he said "like a door slammed"?
qa.a: Shankar felt hurt and shut out, and began to doubt himself, wondering if he was annoying.

qa.q: Which of Shankar's choices help him recover?
qa.a: Admitting the hurt, joining the photography club, choosing not to post a revenge photo and staying polite without chasing the old group.

qa.q: How might the counsellor see Shankar's progress?
qa.a: The counsellor seems encouraged, seeing him reach out to others and resist retaliating.

grounding: A young adult excluded by his friend circle admits the hurt, reaches out to new people, and resists retaliating or blaming himself.

passage:
Saturday night
Ganga's group went to the café again tonight. I saw it on stories. Fourth time this month without me. Nobody said why. I cried in the shower, then felt stupid for crying.
But I'm trying something. First, I'm writing down that it hurts. It does. It really does.
Second, I called Tanvi from my old school. We talked for an hour and she said she'd missed me.
Third, I said yes when the girl in my lab asked if I wanted to join their study group on Monday.
I keep hearing a voice saying, "You're the problem." I'm choosing not to believe it. People drift. It happens.
I thought about making my own group and not inviting Ganga. That would feel good for five minutes. I'm not doing it.
- Avni

qa.q: How many times this month had Ganga's group gone without Avni?
qa.a: It was the fourth time this month.

qa.q: How does Avni feel about being left out?
qa.a: Avni feels hurt and a little foolish for crying, but is determined not to believe the voice saying Avni is the problem.

qa.q: Which of Avni's steps are healthy ways to recover?
qa.a: Admitting the hurt, calling an old friend, joining a new study group, and deciding not to exclude Ganga in return.

qa.q: How might Tanvi have felt getting Avni's call?
qa.a: Tanvi seemed happy and warm, saying she'd missed Avni.

grounding: A young adult excluded by a friend circle admits the hurt, reaches out to others, refuses self-blame and avoids retaliating with exclusion.
